quote: SSE-KMS: customer managed key lets you create/rotate/disable and define access controls; CloudTrail logs GenerateDataKey and Decrypt for SSE-KMS; default encryption context is the object ARN (bucket ARN when Bucket Keys on); S3 Bucket Keys reduce KMS request cost by up to 99 percent; objects under the aws/s3 AWS managed key cannot be shared cross-account; SSE-S3 is the default for new objects since 2023-01-05

AWS managed keys (alias aws/<service>): you can view key policy and audit use in CloudTrail but cannot change properties, rotate, change key policy or schedule deletion; cannot be used cross-account; customer managed keys: full control of key policy, enable/disable, rotation, deletion, CloudTrail audit

SSE-C: S3 never stores the key, you must supply it on every download, key rotation is client-side, AWS managed services cannot decrypt SSE-C objects, HTTPS required; SSE-C disabled by default for new general purpose buckets starting April 2026 (PutBucketEncryption BlockedEncryptionTypes=NONE to enable)

With Bucket Keys: KMS CloudTrail events log bucket ARN instead of object ARN, fewer KMS events, subsequent requests using the bucket-level key do not call KMS or validate against the key policy; bucket-level key fetched at least once per requester; up to 99 percent KMS request cost reduction

SSE-S3: S3 encrypts each object with a unique key and encrypts that key with a key S3 rotates regularly (AES-256 GCM); default for all new uploads since 2023-01-05; no additional charge; no KMS key policy or KMS CloudTrail event involved (supports the SSE-S3 WHY)

Lambda timeout default 3 s, adjustable in 1 s increments up to 900 seconds (15 minutes); Lambda Managed Instances allow 5,400 seconds (90 minutes) for asynchronous and event source mapping invocations

EventBridge Scheduler schedules ECS tasks via the RunTask target with rate, cron (any time zone) or one-time schedules; Fargate launch type selectable; retry up to 185 times, 24 h max retention, optional SQS DLQ
Fargate runs containers without provisioning, configuring or scaling clusters of EC2 instances; new tasks always start on the latest patched platform version revision

Fargate billed per second with a 1-minute minimum (5-minute minimum for Windows), from image download start until the task terminates; us-east-1 Linux/x86 about $0.0404 per vCPU-hour and $0.00444 per GB-hour
AWS Batch supports Fargate compute environments (ECS orchestrator only): no EC2 instances to provision, configure or scale

Lambda Managed Instances run on EC2 managed instances in your account, billable, EC2-based pricing plus a 15 percent management fee, scale to a configured minimum rather than to zero (supports 'runs on EC2 capacity you pay for' in the Lambda WHY)

ALB: you must select at least two Availability Zone subnets, each from a different AZ; ELB creates a load balancer node in each enabled zone; targets in a zone that is not enabled receive no traffic; cross-zone load balancing on by default

When one AZ becomes unhealthy or unavailable, EC2 Auto Scaling launches new instances in an unaffected AZ and rebalances when it recovers; add an AZ by adding its subnet to the group and enabling the zone on the load balancer; ALB requires at least two enabled AZs
Multi-AZ DB instance: synchronous standby replica in a different AZ; standby cannot serve read traffic; existing instance converted by modifying it (ModifyDBInstance) and choosing Multi-AZ

RDS automatically switches to the standby on infrastructure failure without administrative intervention; failover typically 60-120 seconds; the DNS record of the DB instance is changed automatically to point to the standby
Read replicas replicate asynchronously and are for read scaling; you must create them manually; DR use is via promotion to a standalone instance (a manual step), not automatic failover

Cross-Region read replicas supported for Db2, MariaDB, SQL Server, MySQL, Oracle and PostgreSQL; stated use cases include scaling reads into a Region closer to users and DR; higher replication lag than same-Region replicas; data transferred out of the source Region is charged (initial snapshot and every modification); for PostgreSQL a replica is not auto-promoted when the source is deleted
Updates are copied asynchronously to read replicas; read replica in a Multi-AZ deployment: standby replication is synchronous and the standby cannot serve reads, unlike a read replica

Promotion stops replication and reboots the read replica; it becomes a standalone DB instance that can no longer be a replication target; DR pattern = promote, redirect traffic, create a replacement replica
Multi-AZ DB instance standby is synchronous, in a different AZ of the same Region, and cannot serve read traffic

Aurora Global Database: one primary plus up to 10 secondary Regions, replication latency typically under a second; available only for specific Aurora MySQL and Aurora PostgreSQL versions (Aurora feature, not RDS for PostgreSQL)

Visibility timeout default 30 s, max 12 hours; undeleted message becomes visible again for another consumer; retention default 4 days, max 14 days (1,209,600 s); scale on backlog per instance (ApproximateNumberOfMessages / InService instances), raw queue length not proportional; SNS: when delivery policy exhausted 'discards the message—unless a dead-letter queue is attached', HTTP/S total retry time max 3,600 s; Kinesis provisioned shard 1 MB/s or 1,000 records/s write, 2 MB/s read

Read replica use case 'business reporting queries to run against a read replica'; asynchronous replication; 'Unlike a read replica, a standby replica can't serve read traffic'; applications connect to replica like any DB instance; DB instance class change: 'Downtime occurs during this change'; ElastiCache lazy loading / write-through implemented in application code (app checks cache, queries DB on miss, writes cache)

S3 event destinations: SNS topics, SQS queues, Lambda, EventBridge; delivered at least once, typically in seconds; SQS FIFO not supported as S3 destination (use EventBridge); SNS->SQS fanout: messages 'persist in an Amazon SQS queue for other applications to process later'; SQS message invisible to other consumers while in flight, deleted by the consumer that processed it

FIFO: order strictly preserved, no duplicates, message groups for parallel ordered streams, MessageGroupId required; 5-minute deduplication interval; content-based dedup = SHA-256 of body (not attributes); 300 TPS per API action non-high-throughput, 3,000 msg/s with batching (10 per batch), high throughput mode up to 70,000 TPS in us-east-1/us-west-2/eu-west-1; standard queues nearly unlimited TPS; SNS discards after delivery policy unless DLQ; Kinesis per-shard 1 MB/s in, ordering per shard/partition key

Fargate runs containers without provisioning, configuring or scaling EC2 clusters; you specify CPU and memory per task; each task has its own isolation boundary (no shared kernel, CPU, memory or ENI); new tasks always start on the latest patched platform version revision; ECS on Fargate supports ALB/NLB/GWLB with ip target type

ECS target tracking scaling policies add or remove service tasks to keep a metric near target; ALBRequestCountPerTarget is a supported metric (not for blue/green deployment type); scale out fast, scale in gradually

Capacity options: Fargate (pay only for task resources, no infrastructure management, ideal for variable workloads), EC2 instances (you manage instance selection, configuration and maintenance; use for GPU, capacity reservations, specific instance types, privileged capabilities or custom AMIs), ECS Managed Instances
Elastic Beanstalk Docker running on AL2/AL2023 deploys containers to EC2 instances in the environment; ECS-based branch exists for migration from the retired Multi-container Docker AL1 branch

AWS Backup: centralized policy-based backup plans; tag-based resource assignment; copy backups to other Regions on demand or automatically as part of a scheduled plan; cross-account backup via Organizations; AWS Backup Audit Manager provides controls and generates daily compliance reports; Vault Lock enforces WORM; supported resources include EC2, S3, EBS, DynamoDB, RDS, Aurora, EFS, FSx, Storage Gateway, DocumentDB, Neptune, Redshift, Timestream, VMware, CloudFormation, SAP HANA, EKS; AWS Backup does not govern backups taken outside it

Amazon Data Lifecycle Manager automates creation, retention and deletion of EBS snapshots and EBS-backed AMIs only; cannot manage snapshots/AMIs created by other means or instance store-backed AMIs; quota 100 custom policies per Region
S3 replication copies objects between S3 buckets (CRR across Regions, SRR within a Region); live replication does not copy objects that existed before the rule (use Batch Replication)

Backup and restore: RPO in hours, RTO in 24 hours or less (PITR can lower RPO to about 5 minutes in some cases); Pilot light: RPO in minutes, RTO in tens of minutes, databases/object storage always on, application servers not deployed until needed; Warm standby: RPO in seconds, RTO in minutes, scaled-down but fully functional copy always running; Multi-site active-active: RPO near zero, RTO potentially zero, most complex and costly; strategies listed in increasing order of cost and complexity

Pilot light: data replication resources (databases, object storage) always on, application servers switched off / not deployed; promoting an RDS read replica (non-Aurora) takes a few minutes and includes a reboot; Aurora global database replicates with typical latency under a second and a secondary can be promoted in less than one minute; pilot light cannot process requests without additional action, warm standby can handle traffic at reduced capacity immediately; multi-site active/active is the most complex and costly
RDS read replicas replicate asynchronously; cross-Region read replicas supported; promotion to standalone is a manual disaster recovery step; replicas billed as standard DB instances
Promotion reboots the replica and takes a few minutes or longer depending on size; after promotion you direct database traffic to the promoted instance and create a replacement replica

Warm standby: RPO in seconds, RTO in minutes, scaled-down but fully functional copy always running, scaled up at recovery; Pilot light: RPO in minutes, RTO in tens of minutes; Backup and restore: RPO in hours, RTO in 24 hours or less; Multi-site active-active: RPO near zero, RTO potentially zero, most operationally complex; pilot light cannot process requests without additional action first, warm standby can at reduced capacity

Aurora global database: one primary Region for writes and up to 10 read-only secondary Regions; replication latency typically under a second; write forwarding lets secondaries forward writes to the primary; switchover and failover mechanisms to change the primary Region

Aurora global database secondary can be promoted in less than one minute; Route 53 health checks enable automatically initiated DNS failover; Auto Scaling used to scale the DR Region to full production capacity (increase desired capacity); warm standby = scaled down but fully functional copy always on

Active-passive failover uses the failover routing policy: Route 53 answers with the primary while healthy and with the secondary when the primary is unhealthy; active-active uses any other routing policy with health checks

Failover routing = active-passive failover; weighted routing = route traffic to multiple resources in proportions you specify; latency routing = route to the Region that provides the best latency; geolocation routing = route based on the location of your users; multivalue answer = up to eight healthy records at random

With one primary and one secondary failover record Route 53 responds with the primary when healthy and the secondary when unhealthy; for AWS resources with alias records do not create health checks, set Evaluate Target Health to Yes; documented pattern of a web server primary and an S3 website-endpoint bucket secondary holding a temporarily unavailable message; secondary alias target is the S3 website endpoint DNS name

Alias record to an S3 website endpoint requires the bucket name to equal the record/domain name, static website hosting enabled, bucket created by the current account (or specify the Region); S3 website endpoints do not support SSL/TLS, use CloudFront for HTTPS; changes propagate within about 60 seconds; alias queries to AWS resources are free

Both source and destination buckets must have versioning enabled; disabling versioning on the destination makes replication fail (status FAILED); S3 needs an IAM role/permissions to replicate; Object Lock on source requires Object Lock on destination

Replication is automatic and asynchronous; CRR copies objects to buckets in different Regions (compliance distance, latency, operational efficiency); live replication does not replicate objects that existed before the rule, use S3 Batch Replication; S3 RTC replicates 99.99 percent of new objects within 15 minutes under SLA

By default a delete in the source bucket adds a delete marker in the source bucket only, protecting destination data from accidental or malicious deletes; delete marker replication is optional and not supported for tag-based rules; lifecycle-created delete markers are never replicated

S3 One Zone-IA stores data in a single AZ, costs 20 percent less than Standard-IA, 99.5 percent availability, susceptible to data loss if the AZ is lost or damaged; S3 stores data redundantly across a minimum of 3 AZs by default; Intelligent-Tiering monitors access patterns and moves objects not accessed to lower-cost access tiers

S3 object versioning retains the original version before a delete or modification; with S3 replication to a DR Region a source delete adds a delete marker in the source bucket only by default, protecting the DR copy

Span the Auto Scaling group across multiple AZs and attach a load balancer; when an AZ becomes unhealthy or unavailable Auto Scaling launches new instances in an unaffected AZ and redistributes evenly when it recovers; add an AZ by adding its subnet to the group's network settings and enabling that AZ (one subnet per AZ) on the load balancer; ELB creates a load balancer node per enabled AZ; Application Load Balancers must have at least two AZs enabled; internet-facing LB subnets need at least eight free IPs; targets in AZs not enabled for the load balancer receive no traffic

Multi-AZ within a single Region mitigates disasters like fires, floods and major power outages; multi-Region is for the unlikely event that prevents a workload running in a Region; strategies rise in cost and complexity

Each NAT gateway is created in a specific AZ and implemented with redundancy in that zone; if resources in multiple AZs share one NAT gateway and its AZ is down, resources in the other AZs lose internet access; create a NAT gateway in each AZ and configure routing so resources use the NAT gateway in the same AZ; 5 Gbps scaling to 100 Gbps; 55,000 simultaneous connections per IPv4 address per unique destination

AWS recommends NAT gateways over NAT instances (better availability and bandwidth, less administration); NAT gateway: highly available, redundant per AZ, create one per AZ for zone-independent architecture, managed by AWS; NAT instance: use a script to manage failover, you install updates and OS patches, bandwidth depends on instance type

VPC endpoints connect a VPC to endpoint services, AWS services and shared resources over private IPs (interface, gateway for S3/DynamoDB, GatewayLoadBalancer, resource, tunnel, service-network types); traffic stays within the AWS network; internet access is provided by an internet gateway, not endpoints

Multi-AZ DB instance deployment: RDS provisions and maintains a synchronous standby replica in a different AZ; protects against DB instance failure and AZ disruption; the standby cannot serve read traffic; convert an existing instance by modifying it and choosing the Multi-AZ option (modify-db-instance / ModifyDBInstance); higher write/commit latency possible due to synchronous replication

Failover times are typically 60-120 seconds (longer with large transactions or lengthy recovery); failover changes the DNS record of the DB instance to point to the standby, so existing connections must be re-established; automatic failover reasons include primary host unhealthy, network reachability loss, storage failure, OS patching, busy/unresponsive primary, customer modification, reboot with failover; set JVM networkaddress.cache.ttl to 60 seconds or less

Promoting a read replica is user-initiated, reboots the instance and takes a few minutes or longer; the DR procedure is promote, then direct database traffic to the promoted instance, then create a replacement replica

Read replicas replicate asynchronously and are read-only; use cases are read scaling and disaster recovery via promotion; cross-Region read replicas supported; standby replica in Multi-AZ is synchronous and cannot serve reads

Global tables are fully managed multi-Region multi-active replication; any replica can serve reads and writes; low or zero RPO by shifting traffic to another Region if processing is interrupted; asynchronous replication with last-writer-wins conflict resolution (MREC default); MRSC mode exists and is same-account only; no application changes needed (existing DynamoDB APIs)

Aurora global database: writes only to the primary DB cluster in one Region; up to 10 read-only secondary Regions; write forwarding sends secondary write requests to the primary; replication latency typically under a second; failover/switchover needed to make a secondary the writer
RDS read replicas are read-only copies updated asynchronously; cross-Region read replicas supported; promotion to standalone is a manual DR action

S3 replication is asynchronous object copying between buckets; two-way (bi-directional) replication rules keep buckets in sync across Regions for Multi-Region Access Point failover; replica modification sync replicates metadata changes

Active-active failover: any routing policy other than failover (for example latency or weighted) with health checks; Route 53 stops including a record it considers unhealthy and answers with any healthy record

If an alias record points to an AWS resource you cannot set the TTL; Route 53 uses the default TTL for the resource (ELB TTL documented in the ELB request-routing page, 60 seconds); Route 53 does not charge for alias queries to AWS resources

Point-in-time restore creates a new DB instance without modifying the source; RDS uploads transaction logs to S3 every five minutes; LatestRestorableTime is the newest point you can restore to; restore is allowed to any time within the backup retention period

subnet IPv4 CIDR between /28 and /16; first four and last IP of each subnet reserved (network, VPC router, DNS at base+2, future use, broadcast) = 5 addresses

enableDnsHostnames default false unless default VPC, enableDnsSupport default true; private hosted zones in Route 53 and private DNS with interface VPC endpoints require both attributes true

EFS mounts over NFSv4.0/4.1; accessible concurrently from compute in multiple AZs of a Region; one mount target per AZ, file system DNS name resolves to the mount target in the same AZ as the instance; Regional file system has a mount target in each AZ, One Zone file system has a single mount target

Elastic throughput is the recommended default and scales automatically for spiky or unpredictable workloads; General Purpose is the default performance mode; Max I/O not supported with Elastic throughput
